nodes.label: Ismail I
nodes.full: Ismail, shah from 1501, conquered Shirvan, ended the Shirvanshahs' dynasty in 1538 under his son Tahmasp and made Tabriz his capital, with Azerbaijani Turkic as his language of poetry under the pen-name Khatai and Twelver Shiism the state religion; the Qizilbash tribes of Azerbaijan and Karabakh were the base of his power.
nodes.src: Roger Savory, Iran under the Safavids (1980); Vladimir Minorsky, A History of Sharvan and Darband (1958).

nodes.label: Ottoman Caucasus
nodes.full: In the war of 1578–1590, the Ottoman armies of Lala Mustafa Pasha and Osman Pasha took Shirvan, Georgia's Tbilisi, Ganja, Erivan and Tabriz and organised the beylerbeyliks of Shirvan, Çıldır, Tiflis, Erivan and Karabakh; the treaty of Istanbul in 1590 confirmed them. Shah Abbas I reconquered them in 1603–1607.
nodes.src: Peçevi, Tarih; Selaniki; Colin Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300–1650 (2002); Savory 1980.

nodes.label: Shah Abbas I
nodes.full: Shah Abbas I reorganised the Safavid army with slave-soldiers (ghulams) of Georgian, Circassian and Armenian origin, made peace with the Ottomans in 1590, reconquered the Caucasus in 1603–1607, subdued Georgia and moved large numbers of Armenians, Georgians and Muslims into the Iranian heartland. Georgian ghulams such as Allahverdi Khan and Imam Quli Khan rose to be among his chief commanders.
nodes.src: Iskandar Beg Munshi, Tarikh-i alam-ara-yi Abbasi; Savory 1980; David Blow, Shah Abbas (2009).

nodes.label: Georgian kings under two empires
nodes.full: The kings of Kartli (Tbilisi) and Kakheti (Telavi) held their lands as clients of the shah, paying tribute and sending their sons to Isfahan, while those of Imereti and the princes of Samtskhe, Guria and Mingrelia in the west were Ottoman vassals; Simon I of Kartli, Luarsab II, Teimuraz I of Kakheti and the Safavid-appointed Rostom Khan are the best known.
nodes.src: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Vakhushti, Geography of Georgia; Stephen Rapp, Georgian Christian Identity (2003).

nodes.label: Rostom Khan
nodes.full: Rostom Khan, a Georgian Bagrationi brought up at Isfahan and a Muslim, was installed by Shah Safi as king of Kartli in 1633 and held the title until 1658, governing in Persian manner at Tbilisi with the Safavid court's patronage and adopting Georgian customs; his successors Vakhtang V Shahnavaz and Giorgi XI kept the system.
nodes.src: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Vakhushti; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Vakhtang VI
nodes.full: Vakhtang VI, regent from 1703 and king of Kartli from 1716, codified the law of Georgia, founded in 1709 the first press in Tbilisi, patronised poets and scholars, and sought Russian aid when the Safavid state collapsed, and when the Ottomans took Tbilisi in 1723 left for Russia in 1724 with a retinue of about a thousand.
nodes.src: Vakhushti; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Meliks of Karabakh
nodes.full: Five Armenian princes (meliks), of Gulistan, Jraberd, Khachen, Varanda and Dizak, the 'Khamsa', held the highlands of Karabakh as semi-autonomous Safavid vassals under the Karabakh governors, with the catholicos of Gandzasar, the descendants of the Hasan-Jalalian family, as head of the church; their castles and monasteries survived the wars.
nodes.src: Raffi, The Five Melikdoms of Karabagh (1882); Robert Hewsen, 'The Meliks of Eastern Armenia', Revue des études arméniennes (1972–).

nodes.label: Etchmiadzin catholicosate
nodes.full: The catholicosate at Etchmiadzin kept the Armenian church together under Ottoman and Safavid rule, with the patriarchates of Constantinople and Jerusalem and the catholicosate of Sis, and the catholicos Hakob IV and his successors in the seventeenth century petitioned popes and princes for relief and sent an embassy to the west.
nodes.src: Arakel of Tabriz, Book of Histories; Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001).

nodes.label: Safavid khans
nodes.full: After the end of the Shirvanshahs in 1538 the Safavids governed the lands of the Kura and Araxes through beglarbegs and khans from Turkmen tribes, the Ziyadoghlu Qajars at Ganja, the Shamlu and Ustajlu, and tied Karabakh, Shirvan and Erivan into the Safavid administrative provinces; the region's Turkic population was further mixed.
nodes.src: Iskandar Beg Munshi; Savory 1980; Minorsky 1958.

nodes.label: Chaldiran
nodes.full: Selim I's Ottoman army, with muskets and cannon, defeated Ismail's Qizilbash cavalry at Chaldiran on 23 August 1514 and took Tabriz for a few days; the defeat shook Ismail's claim to divinity and fixed the Ottoman–Safavid border in eastern Anatolia and the Caucasus for centuries.
nodes.src: Savory 1980; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: War of 1578–1590
nodes.full: When the Safavid state was weakened by civil strife after Tahmasp's death, the Ottomans took Georgia and Shirvan in 1578 and Tabriz in 1585, and a peace in 1590 left them with most of the Caucasus and Azerbaijan. The war was fought largely by local contingents, Georgians and Turkmen on both sides, and with famine and plague.
nodes.src: Peçevi; Selaniki; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Abbas’s reconquest
nodes.full: From 1603, Shah Abbas retook Tabriz and Nakhchivan, in 1604 took the fortress of Erivan after a siege and in 1606 Ganja and Karabakh, beat the Ottomans at Sufiyan in 1605, and made peace on the basis of the gains at Serav in 1618, so that the Safavids were again masters of the south-east Caucasus.
nodes.src: Iskandar Beg Munshi; Blow 2009.

nodes.label: Murad IV and Erivan
nodes.full: Murad IV took Erivan in 1635, lost it again in 1636 to Safi's army, took Baghdad in 1638 and made peace in 1639 at Zuhab; the last great war of the Safavids and Ottomans fought in the Caucasus left the shah in control of the east and Ottomans of the west.
nodes.src: Evliya Çelebi; Savory 1980; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Kakheti devastated
nodes.full: After Teimuraz I's resistance to his overlordship, Shah Abbas invaded Kakheti in 1614 and 1616, with the burning of towns, the killing of many thousands and the deportation of tens of thousands, some estimates 100,000 or more, to Persia, to Mazanderan and Fereydan; the population of Kakheti is said to have been halved.
nodes.src: Iskandar Beg Munshi; Rapp 2003; Blow 2009.

nodes.label: Great Surgun
nodes.full: As his armies withdrew before the Ottomans in 1604, Abbas ordered a scorched-earth policy and the removal of the population of the Araxes valley and Armenian highlands, Julfa and Erivan among them, to the Persian interior, killing or driving off many; the Armenian historian Arakel of Tabriz tells of many thousands who died on the journey. The deportees were settled at New Julfa and in Mazanderan.
nodes.src: Arakel of Tabriz, Book of Histories (c. 1660); Iskandar Beg Munshi; Savory 1980.

nodes.label: David Bek
nodes.full: Following the Afghan capture of Isfahan in 1722, Armenian forces in Syunik under David Bek and Mkhitar Sparapet held out in mountain fortresses such as Halidzor against Persian and then Ottoman armies, with the Georgian and Russian support they hoped for failing to arrive; David Bek died in 1728 and the resistance faded after Mkhitar's death in 1730.
nodes.src: Hewsen 2001; Raffi, Davit Bek (1882).

nodes.label: Ottoman invasion of 1723
nodes.full: As Safavid power fell, an Ottoman army under Ibrahim Pasha took Tbilisi in June 1723, Erivan in 1724 and for a time Ganja and Shirvan, in a partition of Persia's western lands agreed with Russia by the treaty of Constantinople (1724); Ottoman rule lasted until Nader Shah's recovery in 1735.
nodes.src: Treaty of Constantinople (12 June 1724); Rapp 2003; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Nader’s reconquest
nodes.full: The Afsharid general Nader drove the Ottomans from Azerbaijan, Armenia and Georgia in 1730–1735, concluded with Russia the treaty of Ganja in 1735 by which Russia gave up Baku and Derbent, and in 1736 assembled the great council at Mughan which made him shah; his rule opened a new age in the Caucasus.
nodes.src: Mirza Mahdi Astarabadi, Tarikh-i jahangushay-i nadiri; Michael Axworthy, The Sword of Persia (2006).

nodes.label: Amasya
nodes.full: The first Ottoman–Safavid peace, signed at Amasya in 1555 by Suleiman and Tahmasp, drew the frontier through the Caucasus, giving the Ottomans western Georgia (Imereti, Mingrelia, Guria, Samtskhe), and the Safavids eastern Georgia (Kartli and Kakheti), with Tabriz, Shirvan and Yerevan on the Safavid side. It was the model for later partitions.
nodes.src: Treaty of Amasya (1555); Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Zuhab
nodes.full: The treaty of Zuhab ended the war between Murad IV and Safi in 1639 and fixed the border on the lines of Amasya, with Baghdad to the Ottomans, and Erivan, Karabakh, Shirvan and the east to Persia; it remained in force in its main lines until the Russian wars of the 1800s.
nodes.src: Treaty of Zuhab (1639); Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Law of Vakhtang VI
nodes.full: A commission under Vakhtang VI, then regent, put together between 1705 and 1708 a code, the Dasturlamali of Vakhtang, which codified Georgian customary law, the older laws of Giorgi V and Beqa, the Armenian code of Mkhitar Gosh, Byzantine canons and Muslim law of the time. It became the Georgian legal reference until 1801.
nodes.src: Law of Vakhtang VI (ed. Dolidze); Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Mughan assembly
nodes.full: In January 1736 Nader summoned on the Mughan steppe an assembly of notables, among them Persian khans, Georgian princes and the Armenian catholicos, who elected him shah; Abraham of Crete, the catholicos of Etchmiadzin, attended and was granted privileges for the church.
nodes.src: Mirza Mahdi Astarabadi; Axworthy 2006; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Safavid Shiism
nodes.full: The Safavids imposed Twelver Shiism as the state religion in their lands, suppressing the Sunnis of Shirvan and the Sufi orders and bringing Shia clergy from Lebanon and Bahrain; it became the faith of the Azerbaijani population, with the mourning rites of Muharram at Baku and Shamakhi, while the Ottoman governors of the western provinces held to Sunnism.
nodes.src: Savory 1980; Rula Abisaab, Converting Persia (2004).

nodes.label: New Julfa cathedral
nodes.full: The Armenian deportees of Julfa, with the support of the shah's favour, built churches, schools and a cathedral at New Julfa in Isfahan, the Vank or Cathedral of the Holy Saviour (1655–1664), with Armenian and Persian painting and tiles and with the cathedral's museum and printing press. It is the best monument of the Armenian diaspora.
nodes.src: Vank Cathedral inscriptions; Sebouh Aslanian, From the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean (2011).

nodes.label: Queen Ketevan
nodes.full: Ketevan, mother of Teimuraz I of Kakheti, who had been taken as a hostage to Persia in 1614, was tortured and put to death in Shiraz in 1624 for refusing to abjure Christianity, and is a saint of the Georgian Church; her story was told by Augustinian missionaries and in the poem of her son.
nodes.src: Teimuraz I, The Martyrdom of Queen Ketevan; Augustinian reports from Isfahan (Gouvea, 1606–1626); Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Catholic missions
nodes.full: Italian Theatines, Capuchins and Jesuits and other Catholic missionaries worked in Georgia and Armenia from the early seventeenth century, with houses at Tbilisi, Gori and Akhaltsikhe; they opened schools, translated texts and won a small number of converts, among them in 1710 the writer Sulkhan-Saba Orbeliani, who went to France.
nodes.src: Capuchin and Theatine mission reports; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Teimuraz I
nodes.full: Teimuraz I, king of Kakheti and Kartli, wrote Georgian poems of the 'Martyrdom of Queen Ketevan', 'Joseph and Zulikha' and many lyrics, in imitation of Persian forms, while in exile in Russia and Imereti; he is the first of the poet-kings of late Georgian literature.
nodes.src: Teimuraz I, Poems; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Painters of New Julfa
nodes.full: The Armenian painters of New Julfa, among them Minas, Hovnatan and Hovhannes Mrkuz, combined the manner of Persian painting, European engravings and the Armenian miniature to produce manuscripts, wall-paintings and portraits for the Armenian merchants, and carried forms to Armenia and India.
nodes.src: Aslanian 2011; Sirarpie Der Nersessian, Armenian Art (1977).

nodes.label: Erivan fortress
nodes.full: The Ottoman commander Farhad Pasha rebuilt in 1583 the fortress of Erivan on the Hrazdan with stone walls, towers and artillery, a model of Ottoman provincial fortification; the Safavid khans of the seventeenth century strengthened it, and the Blue Mosque was added in 1765.
nodes.src: Evliya Çelebi, Seyahatname; Iskandar Beg Munshi.

nodes.label: Sulkhan-Saba Orbeliani
nodes.full: Sulkhan-Saba Orbeliani, churchman, diplomat and writer, compiled a dictionary of the Georgian language and a collection of fables and tales, the 'Wisdom of Lies' (Sibrdzne Sitsruisa), and went in 1713–1714 to Rome and Paris to seek aid from Louis XIV; he is the best-known Georgian author of the early eighteenth century.
nodes.src: Sulkhan-Saba Orbeliani, Sibrdzne Sitsruisa and Lexicon (1685–1716); Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Arakel of Tabriz
nodes.full: Arakel of Tabriz, a vardapet and historian, wrote the Book of Histories about 1660 on the events of 1602–1662, including the deportations under Abbas and the life of the Armenians in Julfa and Isfahan, from his own knowledge and eyewitness accounts; it is the main Armenian source for the period.
nodes.src: Arakel of Tabriz, Book of Histories (trans. G. Bournoutian, 2010).

nodes.label: Armenian liberation movement
nodes.full: In 1678 the catholicos Hakob IV and nobles met at Etchmiadzin and sent a mission to Europe to seek help for an Armenian independence; its envoy Israel Ori, a meliks' son from Syunik, spent decades from 1698 at the courts of the elector Palatine, the Habsburgs and Peter the Great, planning an Armenian state under a Western or Russian prince. The plans were not realised.
nodes.src: Israel Ori's letters and memoranda; Hewsen 2001; Ronald Suny, Looking toward Ararat (1993).

nodes.label: Silk and Julfa network
nodes.full: Shah Abbas made the export of raw silk from Gilan, Shirvan and Karabakh a royal monopoly and entrusted it to the Armenian merchants of New Julfa, who built a trading network from Venice, Livorno and Amsterdam to Aleppo, Surat and Manila, using their kinship ties and a system of credit; the silk trade made New Julfa one of the world's major commercial cities.
nodes.src: Aslanian 2011; Savory 1980; Blow 2009.

nodes.label: Baku oil
nodes.full: The oil of the Absheron peninsula, collected from pits and wells and used for lighting, caulking and medicine, and its salt, were exported by caravans and ships across the Caspian and to Persia; European travellers such as Engelbert Kaempfer in 1683 describe the wells and the temple of the fire worshippers at Surakhani.
nodes.src: Engelbert Kaempfer, Amoenitates exoticae (1712).

nodes.label: Ghulams and slave trade
nodes.full: Children and young people from Georgia, Armenia and the Circassian lands were taken in raids, sold or delivered as tribute and sent to the harems and armies of Isfahan and Istanbul, as ghulams of the Safavid army, and as Ottoman household slaves; the slave trade through Akhaltsikhe and the Black Sea ports was a large part of the commerce of the western Caucasus.
nodes.src: Rapp 2003; Savory 1980; Evliya Çelebi.

nodes.label: Presses of Julfa and Tbilisi
nodes.full: The first press in the Safavid lands was set up in 1638 at New Julfa by the bishop Khachatur Kesaratsi, which printed psalters and service books in Armenian; Vakhtang VI founded a Georgian press at Tbilisi in 1709 with type and craftsmen from Wallachia, and printed the Gospels and a Psalter in 1709–1712. The earliest Armenian book had been printed in Venice in 1512.
nodes.src: Aslanian 2011; Rapp 2003; Hakob Meghapart, Urbatagirk (Venice, 1512).

nodes.label: Georgia and Russia
nodes.full: Alexander II of Kakheti swore allegiance to Tsar Fyodor in 1587, the Russians built the fortress of Terek in 1588 on the Caspian shore, and Teimuraz I and later Georgian kings sent embassies to Moscow for aid against Persia; the tsars sent small contingents but did not yet interfere in force.
nodes.src: Rapp 2003; Muscovite embassy records.

nodes.label: Peter’s Persian campaign
nodes.full: Peter the Great's army took Derbent in 1722 and Baku in 1723 at the call of Vakhtang VI and Armenian leaders, and the treaty of St Petersburg in 1723 gave Russia the Caspian provinces; the Russians did not go to Georgia, and in 1735 had to give back the lands.
nodes.src: Treaty of St Petersburg (1723); Rapp 2003; Suny 1993.

nodes.label: Shamakhi earthquake
nodes.full: A great earthquake in November 1667 destroyed Shamakhi, then the capital of the Safavid province of Shirvan and a great silk market, killing many thousands; the administration was moved for a time to nearby Aghsu and trade shifted, and the city was later rebuilt.
nodes.src: Engelbert Kaempfer, Amoenitates exoticae (1712); Minorsky 1958.

nodes.label: Population loss
nodes.full: Wars, deportations, plague and famine reduced the population of eastern Georgia, Armenia and Shirvan in the 1578–1736 period and left much of the land uncultivated, a loss which the chroniclers describe by region and which Nader's reconquest and the Russian conquest later tried to restore.
nodes.src: Arakel of Tabriz; Rapp 2003; Iskandar Beg Munshi.

nodes.label: Georgians of Fereydan
nodes.full: Georgians deported from Kakheti by Abbas were settled in Fereydan in the Zagros mountains, in Mazanderan and in Fars as farmers, soldiers and household slaves, where their descendants, the Fereydani Georgians, kept the Georgian language into the twentieth century.
nodes.src: Iskandar Beg Munshi; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Julfa deportees
nodes.full: According to Arakel of Tabriz, many of the Julfa Armenians drowned crossing the Araxes or died in the cold and from hunger on the march to Isfahan; those who arrived were settled by the Shah in a quarter outside the city that was named New Julfa, with a mayor (kalantar) of their own.
nodes.src: Arakel of Tabriz, Book of Histories; Aslanian 2011.

nodes.label: Ketevan
nodes.full: Ketevan, a queen of Kakheti, was sent to Persia as a hostage, was held in Shiraz, and, according to Georgian and Catholic sources, refused the offer of marriage and conversion by the shah, and was put to death; she is among the best-known Georgian women of the time and her relics were taken to Georgia by Augustinian friars.
nodes.src: Teimuraz I; Gouvea, Relaçam (1611); Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Ismail and Shirvan
nodes.full: In 1500–1501 Shah Ismail defeated and killed the Shirvanshah Farrukh Yasar at Gulistan and then took Baku and Tabriz, founding the Safavid state.
